title: Individual vs Systemic: A Debate About Climate Responsibility

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: I've just switched to a plant-based diet. I read that beef production is responsible for something like 14% of global emissions.

dialogue.speaker: Zoya
dialogue.text: That's a significant step. Though — and I say this as someone who respects the choice — I sometimes wonder whether it really makes the difference we think it does.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: You sound sceptical. Do you not think individual choices matter?

dialogue.speaker: Zoya
dialogue.text: I think they matter somewhat. But when I read that 100 companies are responsible for 71% of global emissions, I feel like we're rearranging deckchairs on the Titanic if we're focusing mainly on whether people eat beef or not.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: But that's a bit of a false dichotomy, isn't it? You can both reduce your personal footprint and campaign for systemic change. They're not mutually exclusive.

dialogue.speaker: Zoya
dialogue.text: Fair point. I just worry that the entire discourse gets hijacked into guilt-tripping individuals, while the corporations doing the most damage get off lightly. There's something a bit convenient about that framing.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: I agree that corporations need to be held accountable. But consumer demand does shape corporate behaviour. If enough people stop buying something, companies change. The EV market is a perfect example.

dialogue.speaker: Zoya
dialogue.text: The EV market is a great example — but it was largely driven by massive government subsidies and mandates, not just consumer preference. Without policy, consumer preference alone wouldn't have been enough.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: True. So maybe the real answer is: individual action, corporate accountability, and government policy all need to happen simultaneously. Not one or the other.

dialogue.speaker: Zoya
dialogue.text: I can agree with that. And I'd add — the political action is the most powerful lever, and that's also an individual choice. Who you vote for, what you campaign for, what conversations you have — those matter enormously.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: So going plant-based and campaigning for a carbon tax are not opposites.

dialogue.speaker: Zoya
dialogue.text: Exactly. And frankly, having made the dietary change yourself probably makes you a more credible voice when you're advocating for policy change.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: I hadn't thought of it that way. That's actually a really useful reframe.

dialogue.speaker: Zoya
dialogue.text: The point is: don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good. Do what you can at the individual level, and use that as a base from which to push for bigger changes.
